slides.title: When Pythagoras is not enough
slides.prompt: Pythagoras needs two known sides and only ever finds a third side. The moment an angle enters the question, sin, cos and tan take over. By the end of this lesson you will have banked 20 marks of real exam working, three of them from actual past papers.

chapter 1 of 5
Naming the sides

Every trig question starts by naming the three sides relative to the marked angle.

Swap opposite and adjacent and both marks are gone before the calculator even opens. The hypotenuse never changes; the other two names depend on which angle is marked.

slides.title: Three sides, three names
slides.prompt: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, as always. The other two names come from the marked angle $\theta$. The side across from $\theta$ is the opposite. The side touching $\theta$ is the adjacent.

visual.content:
chapter 2 of 5
The three ratios

Sin, cos and tan are fixed ratios between pairs of sides, decided entirely by the angle.

SOH CAH TOA: sin is opposite over hypotenuse, cos is adjacent over hypotenuse, tan is opposite over adjacent. Writing the right one with the numbers in is the method mark in every question.

slides.title: One angle fixes the ratio
slides.prompt: The triangle grows and shrinks on its own, and every number moves with it, except one: opposite divided by hypotenuse is stuck at $0.50$. That frozen number belongs to the $30°$ angle and is called $\sin 30°$. Grab the corner and try to shake it loose.

slides.title: Cos does the same with the adjacent
slides.prompt: Same triangle, different pair: now the adjacent and the hypotenuse are highlighted. Their quotient freezes at $0.87$, and that number is $\cos 30°$.

slides.title: Tan pairs the two shorter sides
slides.prompt: The last pair leaves the hypotenuse out entirely: opposite divided by adjacent freezes at $0.58$, which is $\tan 30°$. Three pairs of sides, three ratios, and one angle in charge of all of them.

slides.title: Pick the ratio that connects them

interaction.hint: Name the two sides you have first: one faces $\theta$, one faces the right angle.

config.prompt: You know the side opposite $\theta$ and the hypotenuse. Which ratio connects them?

chapter 3 of 5
Finding a side

One angle and one side are known. Pick the ratio that links them to the side you want.

Worth 2 marks: one for the ratio with the numbers in, one for the value. Check your calculator says degrees before anything else.

interaction.hint: The hypotenuse faces the right angle, and the right angle is the biggest angle in the triangle.

config.prompt: The hypotenuse is $12$ and the angle is $35°$. Before any working, how long can the opposite side $x$ be?

options.whyWrong: Nothing beats the hypotenuse: it faces the largest angle, so every other side is shorter.
Only the hypotenuse is $12$. If another side matched it, the triangle would be squashed flat.

config.successText: Every sin and cos value sits below $1$, which is exactly why the other two sides always come out shorter than the hypotenuse. Keep that as the sanity check for the next slide.

chapter 5 of 5
The exam

The exam dresses these questions in words: angles of elevation, ladders, masts. Find the triangle, then it is the same two lines.

A real past-paper elevation question first, then two full solves with no help.

interaction.hint: Elevation starts from flat. Imagine looking straight ahead first, then tilting your eyes up.

config.prompt: Stand at the blue point and look at the top of the wall. Tap the angle of elevation.

regions.whyWrong: That is the right angle where the wall meets the ground. It is always $90°$, so it is never the elevation.
That is the angle at the top, the depression looking back down. Elevation is measured from where you stand.

config.successText: Elevation is measured up from the flat horizontal to your line of sight. The height and the horizontal distance are then opposite and adjacent, which is why elevation questions are nearly always tan.
